newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Abductions seen rising in "kidnap capital" Manila.
newsitem.headline: Abductions seen rising in "kidnap capital" Manila.

text.p: The Philippine abduction industry is booming, underscoring the country's image as Asia's "kidnap capital", an anti-crime campaigner said on Wednesday.
The kidnapping rate now averaged more than one victim a day, Teresita Ang See, who heads the Movement for the Restoration of Peace and Order, told reporters.
The amount of ransom known to have been paid in the first three months of this year already exceeds the 142 million pesos ($5.4 million) for all of 1996, she said.
"If you count the number of victims it's an average of more than one a day...Now it's anybody," said See.
Ethnic Chinese, one of the country's wealthiest groups, have been the main -- but not the only -- targets of the kidnapping syndicates, 40 of which operate in Manila alone, she said.
"You go out for dinner and no topic is discussed except kidnapping," said See, a Filipino Chinese. As the fear grows, shops in Manila's Chinatown are closing earlier, she added.
"If you own a car and have your own home you are a potential victim. No one is safe," See said.
There is also a high rate of kidnapping on the southern island of Mindanao, where authorities usually blame the crimes on Moslem separatist rebels.
Local newspapers have been referring to the Philippines as the "kidnap capital" of Asia.
National police chief Recaredo Sarmiento has said the monicker is unfair. Police say the kidnapping situation is not as bad as See's group claims.
Police say their main problem is kidnap victims refuse to cooperate with investigations -- often because of suspicion that some police are involved with the kidnapping gangs.
See urged the government to make a far greater effort to deal with the crime, noting that police officers had been implicated in abductions.
Rose Yenko, who chairs the Citizens Action Against Crime, told reporters much of the problem lay in poor training and pay for the country's police force.
Half of police can afford to live only in squatter homes and have little incentive to perform their jobs well, she said.

See said: "It would be a good signal if they prosecuted the higher ups. They keep catching the small fry not the masterminds...It's just musical chairs. (Officials) implicated get put elsewhere instead of being punished."
